questions.stem: At 1000 the nurse gave morphine 4 mg IV push to a client 1 day after a bowel resection who rated pain 8 out of 10. When should the nurse reassess the client's pain and sedation?

options.text: At about 1015 to 1030, at the drug's peak
At 1100, an hour after the dose
At the next scheduled vital signs at 1200
Only if the client uses the call light

rationale.correct: Reassess pain and sedation at the drug's peak: about 15 to 30 minutes after IV and about 60 minutes after oral opioids.

perOption.a: IV opioids peak in about 15 to 30 minutes, when both relief and sedation are greatest.
perOption.b: This misses the peak, when sedation is most likely.
perOption.c: This is too late to judge the effect or catch oversedation.
perOption.d: Reassessment is the nurse's responsibility.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Time pain reassessment after an opioid.

questions.stem: A client with advanced dementia who cannot speak is grimacing, moaning and guarding the right hip 2 days after a hip repair. How should the nurse assess this client's pain?

options.text: Use a behavioral pain scale such as PAINAD
Assume the client is not in pain because the client is not asking
Ask the client to rate the pain on a 0 to 10 scale
Rely on changes in heart rate and blood pressure alone

rationale.correct: Use validated behavioral pain scales for clients who cannot report pain.

perOption.a: Behavioral scales assess breathing, vocalization, facial expression, body language and consolability.
perOption.b: Pain is often undertreated in dementia.
perOption.c: The client cannot use a numeric scale.
perOption.d: Vital signs are unreliable indicators of pain.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Assess pain in a client with dementia.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old sprained an ankle playing basketball 2 hours ago. The ankle is swollen and tender, and an x-ray shows no fracture. Which comfort measure is best right now?

options.text: A wrapped cold pack for 15 to 20 minutes at a time
A heating pad on the ankle for about an hour at a time
Firm massage of the ankle to move the swelling
Letting the foot hang down over the bed

rationale.correct: Use cold for acute injuries in the first 24 to 48 hours and heat later, limiting each application to 15 to 20 minutes.

perOption.a: Cold reduces swelling and pain in the first 24 to 48 hours.
perOption.b: Heat increases swelling in an acute injury.
perOption.c: This can increase swelling.
perOption.d: Elevation reduces swelling.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose heat or cold therapy appropriately.

questions.stem: A client taking sertraline 100 mg daily for depression tells the nurse, "I started St. John's wort last week to give it a boost." The client reports feeling restless and sweaty, with diarrhea. Why is the nurse concerned?

options.text: Together they can cause serotonin syndrome
St. John's wort lowers blood glucose sharply
St. John's wort causes hypothyroidism
St. John's wort makes sertraline weaker

rationale.correct: St. John's wort interacts with SSRIs (serotonin syndrome) and reduces the effect of many drugs, such as oral contraceptives and warfarin.

perOption.a: Both increase serotonin, and restlessness, sweating and diarrhea are early signs.
perOption.b: This is not the main concern.
perOption.c: This is not the concern.
perOption.d: The danger is too much serotonin, not a weaker effect.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with chronic low back pain who takes duloxetine says, "I'd like to try acupuncture along with my medicine." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Let's tell your provider so your care can be coordinated."
"There isn't any evidence that acupuncture helps back pain."
"You'll need to stop the duloxetine before you try acupuncture."
"Go ahead, but there's no need to mention it to your provider."

rationale.correct: Support complementary therapies while making sure the provider knows and screening for interactions.

perOption.a: This respects the client's choice and supports safe, coordinated care.
perOption.b: This is dismissive and inaccurate.
perOption.c: This is not necessary.
perOption.d: Coordination is important.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to interest in complementary therapy.

questions.stem: A nurse who has just started working night shifts says, "I can't sleep during the day." The occupational health nurse gives advice. Which statement by the nurse shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll keep the same sleep times on my days off as far as I can."
"I'll have a strong coffee on my drive home to stay alert."
"I'll use blackout curtains and earplugs when I sleep."
"I'll wear sunglasses on the way home in the morning."

rationale.correct: Shift-work sleep: a consistent schedule, a dark and quiet room, limited morning light and no caffeine late in the shift.

perOption.a: A consistent schedule supports sleep.
perOption.b: Caffeine late in the shift disrupts daytime sleep.
perOption.c: A dark, quiet room supports daytime sleep.
perOption.d: Limiting morning light helps the body prepare for sleep.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client admitted with pneumonia cannot sleep in the hospital and asks for a sleeping pill. The client walks with a walker. What is the nurse's main concern about sedative-hypnotics for this client?

options.text: A higher risk of falls and confusion
A large gain in weight over a short time
A rise in blood pressure the next day
A larger appetite at breakfast

rationale.correct: Avoid sedative-hypnotics in older adults when possible, and try non-drug measures first.

perOption.a: Sedatives impair balance and cognition in older adults (Beers criteria).
perOption.b: This is not the main concern.
perOption.c: This is not the main concern.
perOption.d: This is not the main concern.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client recovering from a bowel obstruction has bowel sounds and passed flatus this morning. The NG tube was removed, and the diet is advanced to clear liquids. The client asks for something to drink. Which item can the nurse offer?

options.text: Apple juice
A cup of milk
Orange juice
Vanilla pudding

rationale.correct: Clear liquids: water, broth, clear juice, gelatin and ice pops; full liquids add milk, pudding and ice cream.

perOption.a: Clear liquids are transparent at room temperature.
perOption.b: Milk is a full liquid.
perOption.c: Juice with pulp is not clear.
perOption.d: Pudding is a full liquid.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose foods for a clear liquid diet.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure on a 2 g sodium diet is choosing lunch from the hospital menu. Which choice best fits the diet?

options.text: Grilled chicken with steamed vegetables
Canned chicken soup with crackers
A ham sandwich with a dill pickle
A slice of frozen pepperoni pizza

rationale.correct: Low-sodium diets: choose fresh foods and limit canned, cured, processed and fast foods.

perOption.a: Fresh, unprocessed foods are low in sodium.
perOption.b: These are high in sodium.
perOption.c: Cured meats and pickles are high in sodium.
perOption.d: Processed foods are high in sodium.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old client newly diagnosed with celiac disease is choosing foods for a family picnic and wants to avoid a flare. Which choice is safe?

options.text: A rice and bean salad
A whole wheat bread roll
A bowl of barley soup
Rye crackers with cheese

rationale.correct: Celiac disease: avoid wheat, barley and rye; rice, corn and certified gluten-free oats are safe.

perOption.a: Rice and beans are naturally gluten-free.
perOption.b: Wheat contains gluten.
perOption.c: Barley contains gluten.
perOption.d: Rye contains gluten.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client with chronic constipation wants to add more fiber to the diet and drinks plenty of water. Which food has the most fiber per serving?

options.text: A cup of cooked lentils
Two slices of white bread
A grilled chicken breast
A cup of plain yogurt

rationale.correct: High-fiber foods: legumes, whole grains, fruits, vegetables and bran, with enough fluid.

perOption.a: Legumes are very high in fiber.
perOption.b: Refined grains are low in fiber.
perOption.c: Meat has no fiber.
perOption.d: Dairy has no fiber.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old client at a wellness visit weighs 90 kg and is 1.75 m tall. The client asks whether the weight is healthy. What is the client's body mass index (BMI)? Round to the nearest tenth.

rationale.correct: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)² = 90 ÷ (1.75 × 1.75) = 90 ÷ 3.0625 = 29.4, in the overweight range of 25 to 29.9.
references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client who had a stroke 3 days ago is awake but has a weak swallow and drools from the left side of the mouth. How should the nurse give oral care?

options.text: Sit the client up and use a soft brush and suction
Lay the client flat and rinse with a large cup of water
Skip oral care until the client can swallow normally
Use a hard toothbrush and plenty of foamy toothpaste

rationale.correct: Oral care for clients with dysphagia: upright or side-lying, minimal fluid and suction at hand.

perOption.a: An upright position and suction prevent aspiration while the mouth is cleaned.
perOption.b: This risks aspiration.
perOption.c: Oral care prevents infection and aspiration pneumonia.
perOption.d: This can injure tissue and cause aspiration.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Provide safe oral care to a client with dysphagia.

questions.stem: A client with dementia in a long-term care unit becomes agitated, shouts and swings an arm at the aide during the morning shower. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop and try a towel bath or a different time of day
Insist on finishing the shower quickly while the client is wet
Ask a second aide to hold the client's arms to finish
Skip bathing for a week until the client is calmer

rationale.correct: Person-centered care in dementia: flexibility, simple steps and a calm approach.

perOption.a: Adjusting the approach reduces distress while meeting hygiene needs.
perOption.b: Forcing care increases agitation and the risk of injury.
perOption.c: Restraining the client is not appropriate.
perOption.d: Hygiene needs must still be met.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Adapt hygiene care for a client with dementia.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old client removes upper and lower dentures before going to sleep in the hospital. How should the nurse store the dentures overnight?

options.text: In a labeled denture cup with water or soaking solution
Wrapped in a paper towel on the bedside meal tray
Dry, in the top drawer of the bedside table until the morning
In a cup of very hot water to disinfect them

rationale.correct: Denture care: clean over a padded sink and store in a labeled cup with liquid.

perOption.a: This prevents warping and loss.
perOption.b: They may be thrown away.
perOption.c: Drying can warp them.
perOption.d: Hot water can warp them.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client has been on bed rest for 10 days after a pelvic fracture. Which complications is the client at risk for because of the immobility? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pressure injuries
Deep vein thrombosis
Constipation
Pneumonia
An increase in muscle mass
Higher bone density

rationale.correct: Immobility affects every system: skin, circulation, lungs, bowels, muscles and bones.

perOption.a: Constant pressure reduces blood flow to the skin.
perOption.b: Venous stasis promotes clotting.
perOption.c: Peristalsis slows.
perOption.d: Secretions pool in the lungs.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is doing passive range-of-motion exercises for a client with left-sided paralysis after a stroke. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Support above and below each joint; stop at resistance or pain
Move each joint a little past the point of pain to stretch it
Move the joints quickly to finish all of them in the time available
Exercise only the right arm and leg, which the client can move

rationale.correct: Passive range of motion: slow, supported and within comfort.

perOption.a: This prevents injury to joints that the client cannot protect.
perOption.b: This causes injury.
perOption.c: Slow, smooth movements are safer.
perOption.d: The affected joints need range of motion most.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client in the ICU has been sedated and on a ventilator for 9 days. Which intervention helps prevent foot drop?

options.text: High-top sneakers or a footboard at 90 degrees
A pillow under the knees to keep both legs relaxed
Sheets tucked in tightly over the toes
Letting the feet rest pointed down for comfort

rationale.correct: Prevent foot drop with neutral ankle positioning and range-of-motion exercises.

perOption.a: This keeps the ankles in a neutral position.
perOption.b: This promotes a knee flexion contracture.
perOption.c: This pushes the feet into plantar flexion.
perOption.d: This promotes foot drop.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is helping a client with right-sided weakness move from the bed to a wheelchair. Place the steps in order, from first to last.

items.text: Place the wheelchair on the client's left (strong) side at a slight angle and lock the brakes
Apply a gait belt around the client's waist
Help the client sit on the edge of the bed with feet flat on the floor
Help the client stand and pivot on the strong leg
Lower the client into the wheelchair

rationale.correct: Transfer toward the strong side, with locked brakes and a gait belt.

perOption.a: The client moves toward the strong side, with the chair secured.
perOption.b: Sitting first lets the blood pressure adjust.
perOption.c: The belt gives the nurse a secure hold.
perOption.d: Pivoting on the strong leg is safest.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with multiple sclerosis is starting a bowel training program at home. When is the best time for the client to try to have a bowel movement each day?

options.text: About 30 minutes after breakfast
Right before going to bed
Whenever the urge happens
On waking, before eating

rationale.correct: Bowel training: the same time daily, after a meal, with fiber and fluids.

perOption.a: The gastrocolic reflex after meals stimulates peristalsis.
perOption.b: This is not the best time.
perOption.c: A set schedule is used.
perOption.d: The meal triggers the reflex.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old resident with severe arthritis and mild dementia is continent when helped to the toilet but often wets before reaching it. The resident's bladder empties completely. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Toileting help every 2 hours and clothes easy to undo
An indwelling catheter to keep the skin dry
Limiting fluids to 500 mL a day to reduce wetting
Adult briefs, changed when the resident is wet

rationale.correct: Functional incontinence: scheduled toileting, easy access to the toilet, simple clothing and skin protection.

perOption.a: Functional incontinence is caused by mobility and thinking barriers, so scheduled help and easy clothing address the cause.
perOption.b: This raises infection risk and is not first-line.
perOption.c: This causes dehydration and concentrated urine.
perOption.d: Briefs do not address the cause.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: While removing a fecal impaction digitally from an 84-year-old client, the nurse notes that the heart rate has dropped from 78 to 48/min and the client looks pale and lightheaded. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop the procedure and assess the client
Finish quickly so the stimulation ends sooner
Give a stimulant laxative and stop for the day
Lower the head of the bed and keep going

rationale.correct: Digital removal can stimulate the vagus nerve; stop if bradycardia occurs and assess the client.

perOption.a: Rectal stimulation can trigger a vagal response with bradycardia.
perOption.b: Continuing worsens the vagal response.
perOption.c: This does not address the bradycardia.
perOption.d: The procedure must stop.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize a vagal response during digital disimpaction.

questions.stem: A client's small-bore feeding tube has stopped flowing after crushed medications were given through it. Tube placement was confirmed this morning. What should the nurse try first?

options.text: Flush gently with warm water using a 60 mL syringe
Flush with cola from the tray to dissolve the clog
Insert the stylet to push through the clog
Use a 3 mL syringe to push the water through hard

rationale.correct: Prevent clogs with regular water flushes and liquid forms of drugs; clear clogs gently with warm water and a large syringe.

perOption.a: Warm water in a large syringe is the first-line way to clear a clog safely.
perOption.b: Acidic drinks can make clogs worse.
perOption.c: This can perforate the tube or the GI tract.
perOption.d: Small syringes create high pressure that can rupture the tube.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.
